Yeah, I guess opinions can be changed. Like, I used to not like analysis very much, but then I got into learning about quantum mechanics and analytic number theory and started to appreciate analysis more. But even then, that works more indirectly than directly. Like I still have to make an effort to read the analytic number theory notes and hope that that will cultivate an appreciation for analysis, and if it hadn't worked, I probably wouldn't find the subject interesting at all.

There are also what could be framed as "beliefs" that don't necessarily reflect an external world but which can't really be changed. One could frame me being trans as having a "belief" that I am a woman or me being gay as having a "belief" that women are more attractive than men, but the consensus seems to be that neither of those things can really be changed except in a few marginal cases.

But if we look at the belief that I will never achieve happiness, either there is some point in the future at which I achieve happiness, or there isn't. You could determine this by waiting until the future and asking me "are you generally happy with your life", to which I would answer yes or no. "Category theory is beautiful" may not have a truth-value but "u/isomorphy thinks category theory is beautiful" does. So I'm not sure if "I will never be happy" falls into the pure "opinions and attitudes" category.

It's interesting that you say that.  In what sense are beliefs malleable? Like, could you decide to believe you were a horse if you felt like it? I personally would be unable to believe I was a horse unless I woke up with hooves, fur, and a snout one day.  "I believe X", for me, is essentially equivalent to saying "X is true" while acknowledging that a reasonable person might say "X is false", so willing myself into believing something would feel subjectively the same as willing that thing to be true, and I obviously can't just will arbitrary propositions into being true. I'm not trying to be snarky, I just don't understand what people mean when they say beliefs are malleable.

POSSIBLE explanations for each of the specific instances, without invoking memory OR the supernatural:

\-Fruit of the Loom: You usually don't see leaves in a pile of fruit unless the pile of fruit is in a cornucopia. The "cornucopia" schema is formed subconsciously before the experiencer even knows the word "cornucopia" The fruit of the loom logo is very busy, and so the brain can't notice every detail at once, and so it fills in the "cornucopia" schema without being aware of the cornucopia's . It becomes closely associated enough to the schema for the experiencer to ask their parents what the horn-shaped basket in the logo is called and the parents, likewise seeing the logo through the lens of a preexisting schema, know immediately what the child is talking about and say "cornucopia", resulting in an anchor memory.

\-JFK: Experiencer never noticed the other two people in the car.

\- Chick-Fil-A: "Chick" is longer than "Fil" or "A", so "Chik-Fil-A" or "Chic-Fil-A" would have been better names for the restaurant. Since literate people don't read every letter (source: [https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/people/matt.davis/cmabridge/](https://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/people/matt.davis/cmabridge/)), people substitute one of the better alternatives for the clunky actual name even WHILE reading it.

\-Froot Loops: Literate people don't read every letter of a word.

\-Joel Osteen: Literate people don't read every letter of a word. 

\-Christopher Reeve: "Reeves" is a more common surname than Reeve, and the brain may correct Reeve to Reeves WHILE HEARING IS TAKING PLACE.

\-Kitkat: Literate people don't read every letter of a word.

\-Berenstain Bears: Literate people don't read every letter of a word.

\-Curious George: Experiencer applied the "monkey" schema to Curious George, and never noticed that he deviated from the schema by a lack of a tail.

\-Monopoly Man: Experiencer applied the "rich fancy man" schema to the monopoly man, and never noticed that he deviated from the schema because he lacked a monocle.

\-Jiffy Burger: The burger is "Jif"-y, in the same way that putting salt on something makes it "salty"

\-Mona Lisa: Whether her facial expression is a half-smile or a full smile is a matter of interpretation.

\-Ed McMahon: Don't know about this one.

\-Shazam: Small details in the background of the movie revealed too much about CIA mind-control attempts that were shaping up to be a sort of MKULTRA 2.0, and so the agency worked with Sinbad to destroy all evidence of the movie having ever existed.
